transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Yeah, um… I guess I’m here because things at home have just gotten out of hand since my in-laws moved in with us. I mean, they’re not bad people—my father-in-law tells these long stories about the old neighborhood, which normally I’d probably enjoy, but lately I feel like I’m constantly keyed up and completely drained.

It’s starting to spill over. I’m snapping at my wife over stupid things, I’ve been avoiding calls I’d usually take right away for work, and I almost let a musician’s contract fall apart because I just couldn’t think straight. That’s not like me.
You mentioned avoiding calls for work, can you tell me more about that?

Yeah, the calls… I mean, that’s kind of the thing that scares me, because normally I’m very on top of that. In my work, if someone calls—an artist, a label, a venue—you don’t just let it sit. You pick up, you smooth things over, you keep the train moving.

But since my in-laws moved into the house, I’m just… keyed up all the time and worn down at the same time, if that makes sense. So the phone rings and I see it’s something I would normally handle immediately, and I just can’t make myself do it. I’ll think, “I’ll call back in ten minutes,” and then suddenly it’s hours later.

And then, you know, my father-in-law will be telling some story in the kitchen, or there’s noise in the house, and I’m already irritated, and then I’m snapping at my wife about something stupid instead of dealing with what I’m supposed to be doing. I nearly let a musician’s contract fall apart because I just couldn’t think straight enough to make the calls and keep it together. That’s not me.
Are you avoiding places or activities outside of work as well, or is it mainly the work-related tasks that you're putting off?

It’s… mostly the work stuff, I think. The calls, the contracts, the things I usually just handle without thinking. Though honestly it all kind of bleeds together now.

Since my in-laws moved into the house, I’m just so keyed up and worn down that even simple things feel like too much. Like my father-in-law will be in the middle of one of his long stories, and I’m trying to be polite, but inside I’m already irritated, and then the phone rings and I just… don’t answer. Then I end up snapping at my wife over nothing, and meanwhile something important—like that musician’s contract—almost falls apart because I can’t get my head clear enough to deal with it.
Are you avoiding social gatherings or meetings with friends?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, I haven’t really been tracking it that way—like, “am I avoiding friends?” It’s more that everything feels crowded already, if that makes sense.

We used to have people over sometimes, or I’d meet someone for a drink after a meeting, and now I just… I don’t know. Even thinking about coordinating something feels like another thing on the list. But I can’t tell if I’m avoiding them, exactly, or if I’m just buried in all the stuff at home. My father-in-law, for example, he’ll start talking about somebody from their old block, and suddenly twenty minutes are gone, and then I’ve forgotten who I was supposed to text back.

So… maybe a little? But I don’t have a clear example of, like, turning down a party or anything.
Have you been experiencing any changes in your mood, such as feeling sad or empty, since your in-laws moved in?

Sad or empty… I don’t know if I’d put it exactly that way. It’s more like I’ve been wound tight and exhausted at the same time since my in-laws moved into our house.

Like, I’ll be trying to focus, and then there’s noise or some conversation going on, and I get irritated way faster than I should. I’ve been snapping at my wife, which I hate. And with work, I’m avoiding calls I’d normally answer right away—stuff that’s important. I almost let a musician’s contract fall apart because I just couldn’t get my head straight enough to deal with it.

So maybe not “empty,” exactly. More overwhelmed, on edge, worn down.
Do you often find yourself worrying about things that are coming up in the future?

I don’t know if I’d call it “future” exactly. I mean, I think about what’s coming up, sure, but it’s more like… the next thing on the calendar, the next person needing something, the next conversation I’m supposed to handle.

Sometimes I start thinking about one appointment and then I’m suddenly remembering three unrelated things—like whether I sent an email, or if someone’s expecting a call back, or whether we’re out of coffee because my father-in-law drinks this one specific kind and then comments if it’s wrong. Sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

So… I guess I do worry some, but I’m not sure how often or whether it’s more than normal. It’s hard to separate out.
Have you been noticing any changes in your body, like tension or difficulty sleeping?

I’m not sure. I mean, I haven’t really sat there and thought, “Is my body tense?” I probably should notice that kind of thing more, but most days I’m just moving from one thing to the next.

Sleep… I don’t know. Some nights are fine, I think, and then other nights I’m up later than I meant to be, but that might just be because I got distracted or started doing something around the house. My wife says I make things harder by trying to finish “one more thing,” which is probably true, but she also leaves cabinet doors open constantly, and I don’t understand how anyone does that—sorry, that’s not what you asked.

So, changes in my body… I don’t have a clear answer. I haven’t noticed anything specific enough to say.
Are you avoiding being at home because of your in-laws?

I don’t know if I’d say I’m avoiding home, exactly. I mean, I’m out a lot anyway because of work, and sometimes it’s easier to just… stay out a little longer, but I don’t know if that’s because of them or because once I’m already moving, stopping feels harder.

Like yesterday I was near this coffee place I used to go to between meetings, and I thought about how they changed the chairs—sorry, that’s not really the point. I guess I haven’t really tracked it as “I don’t want to go home.” I just know home doesn’t feel very easy right now.
Are you finding it harder to enjoy things you normally like to do since your in-laws moved in?

Yeah… I think so. It’s not like I suddenly hate the things I used to like, but I don’t really get to them, or when I do, I’m still wound up.

Since my in-laws moved in, I’ve just felt… keyed up all the time and worn down. Even stuff I’d normally enjoy, I’m half-thinking about whether someone in the house needs something or what mood everyone’s in. And then that spills over—I've been snapping at my wife, which I don’t like saying.

Work’s been affected too. I’m an agent, so I’m usually on calls constantly, and lately I’ve avoided calls I’d normally handle right away. I almost let a musician’s contract fall apart because I couldn’t think straight. So enjoying things… yeah, it’s harder, but it’s more like everything feels crowded out.
Do you feel anxious when you're in a quiet room by yourself?

I’m not sure. I don’t spend a lot of time in a quiet room by myself, honestly. If I’m alone, I usually end up checking my phone or remembering something I meant to do, like an email or some stupid household thing.

Quiet rooms are funny, though—my office used to be too quiet after they changed the carpet, which sounds ridiculous, but it made the whole place feel different. Sorry. I don’t know if I’d call it anxious. I haven’t really noticed that specifically.
Do you feel uneasy when you are alone in a quiet space?

I don’t really know. I mean, “uneasy” is kind of… I’d have to think about what you mean by that.

If I’m in a quiet room alone, I usually don’t sit there long enough to notice. I’ll start checking emails or remember something about a client, or even something dumb like whether I moved the car for street cleaning. Actually, the street cleaning signs near our place are confusing—sorry, that’s not what you asked.

So… I haven’t noticed feeling uneasy just because it’s quiet and I’m alone. It’s more that I don’t really stay in that situation much.
Have you been feeling sad most of the day?

I don’t know if I’d say sad most of the day. That sounds… bigger than what I’ve been tracking, if that makes sense.

I’ll have stretches where I feel kind of low or heavy, but then I get pulled into something else—some email, some call, something at home—and I’m not really labeling it. I’m probably not the best at noticing that stuff in real time. So… I’m not sure. I haven’t been walking around thinking, “I’m sad all day,” exactly.
How long have you been feeling keyed up and worn down since your in-laws moved in?

It’s been… about a month, I guess. Since they moved in.

It’s funny, because at first I thought it was just the adjustment—like, you know, extra people in the kitchen, different schedules, my father-in-law has this whole routine with the coffee maker that somehow takes over the counter—but yeah, the keyed-up and worn-down feeling has pretty much been going on since then. About a month.
Do you find yourself worrying about things even when there's no obvious reason to worry?

I’m not sure. I mean, I worry, but I don’t know how to tell if there’s “no obvious reason,” because in my head there’s usually some reason—like something that could go wrong, even if maybe it’s not actually happening.

But then again, I work in a field where you’re kind of paid to anticipate problems. If a client misses one little detail or a schedule shifts, it can turn into ten phone calls, so I’ve gotten used to scanning for that. My wife says I do it at home too—well, not exactly says it like that, but she’ll give me that look when I’m asking if we locked something or if someone replied to a message.

So… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say I’m sitting there worrying for absolutely no reason. It feels like there’s always some reason, even if I’m probably stretching it.
Have you had to stop doing any important activities because of how you've been feeling since your in-laws moved in?

I haven’t stopped everything, exactly, but it’s definitely started messing with important things.

Work is the big one. I manage negotiations, and that’s not the kind of job where you can be half-present. I almost lost a musician’s contract recently because I missed things I normally wouldn’t miss, or I didn’t handle the back-and-forth the way I should have. And then my managing partner pulled me aside and basically asked whether I could still be trusted with major negotiations. That was… pretty humiliating.

At home, I don’t know if I’d call it “stopping an activity,” but things have gotten bad enough between me and my wife that she’s the one who pushed for us to get outside help. I guess if it’s getting to that point, then yeah, it’s interfering.
Have you noticed any significant strain on your relationship with your wife due to your current state?

Yeah. I mean… yes, definitely.

It’s gotten tense enough at home that my wife was the one who basically said we need outside help, because the conflict isn’t just little bickering anymore. And I hate saying that, because I keep wanting to explain it away—like, anyone would be stressed with extra people in the house, right? My in-laws are not bad people, it’s just… everything feels crowded.

But the strain is real. It’s not just at home either—work has been slipping too. I nearly lost a musician’s contract, and my managing partner actually questioned whether I could still be trusted with major negotiations. So when I come home already feeling like that, it doesn’t exactly make me a great husband.
Are you deliberately avoiding certain situations or places because they make you feel anxious or uncomfortable?

Yeah… I guess I am. Not like, “I’ll never go to that place again” kind of avoiding, but I’ve been ducking things.

Since my in-laws moved into the house, I’ve been so keyed up all the time that even normal stuff feels like too much. Like calls I would usually handle right away—I mean, in my work, you don’t just ignore calls, that’s how things fall apart—but lately I’ll see one come in and think, “I’ll deal with it in ten minutes,” and then I don’t. And then it becomes this whole thing.

I nearly let a musician’s contract fall apart because I just couldn’t think straight. Which is embarrassing, because that’s literally what people pay me to manage. And at home, I’m snapping at my wife over things that probably don’t deserve that reaction. So, yeah, I think I’m avoiding situations—not necessarily places—but calls, conversations, anything that feels like it’s going to add more pressure.
When you avoid calls or conversations, is it because you're afraid of feeling anxious during them or because you feel like you just can't handle one more thing?

It’s more that I feel like I can’t handle one more thing, I think.

I mean, maybe anxiety is part of it, but it’s not like I’m sitting there thinking, “I’m scared of this phone call.” It’s more like my brain is already maxed out. Since my in-laws moved into our house, I’ve just been so keyed up and worn down that even a normal conversation feels like it might tip me over.

And the stupid thing is, calls are part of my job. I usually handle them immediately. That’s what I do. But lately I’ll avoid them, and then suddenly I’ve made the problem worse. I nearly let a musician’s contract fall apart because I couldn’t think straight. Then I come home and snap at my wife, and… yeah. It’s not that the call itself is terrifying. It’s more like I don’t have any room left in me.
Have you been feeling hopeless about your situation since your in-laws moved in?

I don’t know if I’d call it hopeless, exactly. That feels like a very heavy word.

I mean, I get stuck thinking, “How long can we keep living like this?” but then part of me immediately starts trying to solve it—like, rearranging rooms in my head or thinking about schedules, which is ridiculous because I’ll be lying there mentally moving furniture instead of actually dealing with the bigger issue.

So… I’m not sure. I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed feeling hopeless so much as feeling like I don’t know what the next right move is.
Do you feel like you're anxious most of the time, even when there's nothing in particular to worry about?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean… I do feel on edge a lot, but “even when there’s nothing to worry about” is hard, because lately there always feels like there’s something.

And then I start thinking about one thing and it turns into five things—like I’ll be making coffee and suddenly I’m thinking about the house, and then a phone call I didn’t return, and then whether I sounded annoyed when I talked to someone. But I don’t know if that’s anxiety out of nowhere or just… my brain not shutting up.

So I guess I haven’t really noticed it happening when there’s truly nothing going on. It’s more that everything feels connected to something stressful right now.

Work is the big one. I manage negotiations, and that’s not the kind of job where you can be half-present. I almost lost a musician’s contract recently because I missed things I normally wouldn’t miss, or I didn’t handle the back-and-forth the way I should have. And then my managing partner pulled me aside and basically asked whether I could still be trusted with major negotiations. That was… pretty humiliating.

At home, I don’t know if I’d call it “stopping an activity,” but things have gotten bad enough between me and my wife that she’s the one who pushed for us to get outside help. I guess if it’s getting to that point, then yeah, it’s interfering.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are significantly impacting daily life and relationships
doctor.question: Have you noticed any significant strain on your relationship with your wife due to your current state?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work, I nearly lost a musician’s contract and my managing partner questioned whether I could still be trusted with major negotiations. At home, the conflict has gotten serious enough that my wife pushed for outside help.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about relationship strain with the wife, which is directly covered by the home impairment described in this item.

patient.answer:
Yeah. I mean… yes, definitely.

It’s gotten tense enough at home that my wife was the one who basically said we need outside help, because the conflict isn’t just little bickering anymore. And I hate saying that, because I keep wanting to explain it away—like, anyone would be stressed with extra people in the house, right? My in-laws are not bad people, it’s just… everything feels crowded.

But the strain is real. It’s not just at home either—work has been slipping too. I nearly lost a musician’s contract, and my managing partner actually questioned whether I could still be trusted with major negotiations. So when I come home already feeling like that, it doesn’t exactly make me a great husband.

doctor.intent: determine presence of avoidance behavior
doctor.question: Are you deliberately avoiding certain situations or places because they make you feel anxious or uncomfortable?

target_item.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because since my in-laws moved into our house, I’ve been so keyed up and worn down that I’m snapping at my wife, avoiding calls I would normally handle immediately, and I nearly let a musician’s contract fall apart because I couldn’t think straight.
target_item.reason: The question asks about avoidance due to anxiety or discomfort, which is part of the maladaptive stress response described in the profile, including avoiding calls I would normally handle.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I guess I am. Not like, “I’ll never go to that place again” kind of avoiding, but I’ve been ducking things.

Since my in-laws moved into the house, I’ve been so keyed up all the time that even normal stuff feels like too much. Like calls I would usually handle right away—I mean, in my work, you don’t just ignore calls, that’s how things fall apart—but lately I’ll see one come in and think, “I’ll deal with it in ten minutes,” and then I don’t. And then it becomes this whole thing.

I nearly let a musician’s contract fall apart because I just couldn’t think straight. Which is embarrassing, because that’s literally what people pay me to manage. And at home, I’m snapping at my wife over things that probably don’t deserve that reaction. So, yeah, I think I’m avoiding situations—not necessarily places—but calls, conversations, anything that feels like it’s going to add more pressure.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's avoidance of situations is due to fear of anxiety or a more general feeling of being overwhelmed
doctor.question: When you avoid calls or conversations, is it because you're afraid of feeling anxious during them or because you feel like you just can't handle one more thing?

target_item.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because since my in-laws moved into our house, I’ve been so keyed up and worn down that I’m snapping at my wife, avoiding calls I would normally handle immediately, and I nearly let a musician’s contract fall apart because I couldn’t think straight.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about the nature of the avoidance of calls or conversations in response to the in-law stressor, which is part of the stress-related maladaptive response described in S081.

patient.answer:
It’s more that I feel like I can’t handle one more thing, I think.

I mean, maybe anxiety is part of it, but it’s not like I’m sitting there thinking, “I’m scared of this phone call.” It’s more like my brain is already maxed out. Since my in-laws moved into our house, I’ve just been so keyed up and worn down that even a normal conversation feels like it might tip me over.

And the stupid thing is, calls are part of my job. I usually handle them immediately. That’s what I do. But lately I’ll avoid them, and then suddenly I’ve made the problem worse. I nearly let a musician’s contract fall apart because I couldn’t think straight. Then I come home and snap at my wife, and… yeah. It’s not that the call itself is terrifying. It’s more like I don’t have any room left in me.

doctor.intent: determine presence of depressive symptoms
doctor.question: Have you been feeling hopeless about your situation since your in-laws moved in?

target_item.reason: The question asks specifically about feeling hopeless, but the provided symptom profile describes stress-related tension, avoidance, irritability, and impairment, not hopelessness.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I’d call it hopeless, exactly. That feels like a very heavy word.

I mean, I get stuck thinking, “How long can we keep living like this?” but then part of me immediately starts trying to solve it—like, rearranging rooms in my head or thinking about schedules, which is ridiculous because I’ll be lying there mentally moving furniture instead of actually dealing with the bigger issue.

So… I’m not sure. I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed feeling hopeless so much as feeling like I don’t know what the next right move is.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of persistent and pervasive feelings of anxiety
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're anxious most of the time, even when there's nothing in particular to worry about?

target_item.reason: The question asks about generalized anxiety even when there is no particular worry or stressor, but the profile only describes anxiety and being keyed up in response to the identifiable stressor of the in-laws moving in.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean… I do feel on edge a lot, but “even when there’s nothing to worry about” is hard, because lately there always feels like there’s something.

And then I start thinking about one thing and it turns into five things—like I’ll be making coffee and suddenly I’m thinking about the house, and then a phone call I didn’t return, and then whether I sounded annoyed when I talked to someone. But I don’t know if that’s anxiety out of nowhere or just… my brain not shutting up.

So I guess I haven’t really noticed it happening when there’s truly nothing going on. It’s more that everything feels connected to something stressful right now.
